utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. May we have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dan Saxon, Mark Harmon, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all the parties to the proceedings. The Defence of Mr. Perisic are represented by Novak Lukic, Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith, and Boris Zorko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. For the record, we're still sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis, in Judge Picard's absence. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence wishes to call its first witness, Mr. Miodrag Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated sir. Good morning to you, sir, and ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody else present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Let me first ask you to state your name for the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: My name is Miodrag Simic, colonel general of the Army of Yugoslavia, retired since the 1st of January, 2002. My last position was that of the commander of the 1st Army of the -- for army of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have already given an answer that I wanted to elicit among the first things. It has to do with your career. I have already mentioned to you something -- with which you already have experience because you have already testified before this Tribunal. In which case did you testify, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I testified before this Tribunal in the Ojdanic case as a Defence witness. As far as I remember, it was in September 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank. While we were preparing for this examination you told me that even then that you knew once you are asked a question in a language you understand, you're supposed to wait for a short while, and the same applies to me, to enable the interpreters to interpret everything for the transcript. You started off at a very good pace. Just please bear in mind to pause a -- for a short while before you answer my question, and you also have the transcript on the screen in front of you. I will try to go through the most important elements of your career briefly. I hope the Prosecution won't object to my leading the witness in these matters to save time. You graduated from the Military Academy in 1965, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1975, you were sent to the Command Staff Academy of the army --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't receive a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1975, you were sent for training to the Command Staff Academy.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I completed my training there in the period from 1976 through 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before that, during that time you were serving with army units in -- in the 2nd Army, at several places in the area of the Pristina garrison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I arrived there with a rank of lieutenant in 1970. And I left as lieutenant-colonel in 1984.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then you were transferred to Belgrade and you were appointed to the position of inspector of combat readiness in the chief inspectorate of national defence?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, of the armed forces of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. I wasn't as precise as you expected me to be but I will improve. From 1986 you started working in the General Staff of the JNA first, which later became the army of Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At first, you were an administrative officer in the 1st department for planning and the use of the armed forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1988, you were promoted to the rank of colonel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1990, you became head of the department for combat readiness and for the planning of combat readiness in the same organisational unit as the General Staff -- of the General Staff in the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then you became chief of the department for planning and combat readiness in the 1st Administration of the -- sorry, first department of the 1st Administration; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Later you became chief of department for doctrine and development; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then in 1993, you became chief of department for planning and combat readiness, and, at the same time, deputy of the administration for operations of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I must add, that that -- that year I also became head of the 1st Administration in November.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The information that I had was that this was in 1994. So that in December you became chief of the 1st Administration with the rank of Major-General.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: In December 2003 [as interpreted], I was appointed to that position based on the order of the Chief of General Staff. I had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... witness say December 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So when were you promoted, Major-General?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: You cannot be promoted to the rank of general without a decree. In March, roughly, the President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia issued a decree appointing me chief of the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You remained in that position until June 1996, when you were appointed Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army of the army of Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... does the decree facilitate your promotion to a general or does it appoint you as chief of administration? We got two separate, different answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I suppose you understood the Judge Moloto's question.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, for a colonel to be promote to the rank of general, there must be an establishment position, a vacant establishment position and there must be a decree to that effect because generals are appointed by the President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, by his decree. The Chief of General Staff issued an order to appoint me to my new position in November 1993. If I had remained in that status, I wouldn't have been able to get the rank of general. I don't know -- general. I don't know whether I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1999, you were appointed to the position of councillor of the Ministry of Defence as lieutenant-general; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the same year, you became the assistant Chief of Staff of the army of Yugoslavia for the army, the land forces, with a rank of lieutenant -- sorry, colonel general.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The same year, I became assistant Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command for the land forces with the rank of lieutenant-general. But the establishment position is such that this is a position for a colonel general.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, we will later analyse the notion of the staff of the Supreme Command. But was that during the period of the military intervention in Kosovo? Is that how we should understand the -- the phrase "staff of the Supreme Command"?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But this is really still the General Staff but due to the changed circumstances, the term changed.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: It is defined by our rules and regulations that the General Staff, at times of imminent threat of war, or, in a state of war, is transformed from General Staff to the staff of the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And we are now moving closer to the end. In 2000, you became assistant Chief of General Staff for the army of Yugoslavia for operational and staff matters -- sorry, in the section for operational staff matters; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And finally, what you said at the very beginning, in 2001, you became commander of the 1st Army of the army of Yugoslavia. And you were discharged from service on the 31st of December, 2001, when you retired.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Simic, let us first speak about the General Staff in general terms. But let us first try to explain what the General Staff was like in the SFRY and later. Can you tell me in a few words, since at that time, too, you were in the General Staff of the JNA, how the structure was and what the hierarchy was there.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: While the JNA was in existence, the General Staff of the JNA was one of the establishment units of the Federal Secretariat of People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. What was the SSNO at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The Federal Secretariat of People's Defence, SSNO, with regard to the chain of command was directly linked with the Presidency of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That means that the General Staff was not in the chain of command immediately after the Presidency of the state, but it was immediately below the minister of -- of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But then the minister of defence was called federal secretary of People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And the institution was called Federal Secretariat of People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was the federal secretary and who was the Chief of General Staff then?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Veljko Kadijevic, colonel general, was the federal secretary; and Blagoje Adzic, also colonel general, was Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What changed in the structure when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was established and when new constitution and regulations were passed and regulated military structures?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: When the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was established and when it passed its constitution in terms of the command of the army, the chain of command was substantially changed. The Chief of the General Staff was no longer subordinated to the federal minister of defence but, rather, it was subordinated to the Supreme Defence Council as a collective body in command of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there a body which was a new body with regard to the Federal Secretariat of National Defence?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I wanted to be brief. However, when the constitution was passed, that had an impact on the chain of command. And between the secretariat and the minister of defence, there was no longer the relationship of subordination but, rather, mutual cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was the minister of defence subordinated to? In what structure was that body?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence was one of the ministry's of the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who the minister of defence was when the ministry was established at --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: At that time, it was the late Pavle Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to the relationship between the ministry and the General Staff. But now I would like us to look at the Law on Army of Yugoslavia and particularly some articles that we already saw in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But now I'd like to call up P197, page 1 in B/C/S and page 2 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, could you please look at the articles. If you can't see the picture on the screen, we have a hard copy of everything.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I would prefer a hard copy. The screen is too far. However if I invest some effort, I will --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This seems to be the only document that we don't have a hard copy of but we'll try and enlarge the letters. Please look at Article 3. I'm sure that you know it by heart. General, you know everything that we're going to discuss, almost by heart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... assist the witness, try to get the screen closer to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have the adequate page. It -- it is probably adequate but can we scroll down the B/C/S page, and blow up the bottom right-hand side corner, yes, Article 3, this is what I wanted. And Article 4 as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I can assist, Your Honour. I believe I have a copy in B/C/S, if that would assist the witness, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With pleasure, and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I would welcome your comment on Article 3 of the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia. Let's not read it. We have it on the screen. But can you please tell us briefly what the article is about.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: This Article of the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia deals with the command in the army and it says that it shall be based on the basic and elementary principle which is the principle of unity of command when it comes to the use of the forces and materiel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is emphasised that this refers to the use of the forces and materiel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to that as well. Let's move on to Article 4 which is again very precise and speaks about the position and role of the President of the Republic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Given the previous article that we just mentioned, Article 3, what was the position of the supreme commander, in terms of the use of the forces and materiel?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as the President of the Supreme Council of Defence had an exclusive and inalienable right to command and use the Army of Yugoslavia in peacetime and in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then, further on, it -- it is stipulated what the President of the Republic does when it comes to the command of the army. I'm not going to dwell upon that, but we can see that the term "command" is clearly emphasised when it comes to the use of the forces and materiel. And now let's move on to Article 5. I apologise. Please read it, or, actually, I would kindly ask you to comment upon each and every paragraph in this article, because it is very important.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Article 5 reads: "The General Staff of the army shall be the highest professional and staff organ for the preparation and use of the army in times of peace and war. "The Chief of the General Staff, in accordance with the basic principles of organisation, development and establishment of the army and the documents issued by the President of the Republic, shall do the following. "Firstly, determine the organisation, plan of development, and establishment of the commands, units, and institutions of the army."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's stop here for a moment. Let's pause. Could you please comment on what you have just read, the definition of the General Staff, and the main form of the functioning of the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: You asked me about my position as the assistant Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command for land army. This means that the General Staff was the highest staff organ for the preparation and use of the army in times of peace and war. The Chief of the General Staff was the top person in the army and the army organisation, and as such, it did not have the right to use the -- the army without prior consent or, rather, decision of the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In simpler terms, did the general -- the Chief of the General Staff have the right to issue an order or command the use of the forces?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I have to provide a clarification at this point. If, when we say the use of a unit, if we imply manoeuvre training, alerts, combat, mobilisation, and verification, then the answer would be yes, because these are the elements that constitute preparations for combat. When it comes to the use of the force for which it -- it was prepared, it doesn't have the right because this is within the exclusive purview of the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Bear with me, I have to check the transcript. Could you please clarify the following. In the sentence, page 12, when you said alert for combat, could you please clarify that -- could you please clarify this for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... doesn't say alert for combat. It says manoeuvre, training, alerts, combat, mobilise, and verification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes, that's correct. Then everything is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your explanation was good, General. We have no problem there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is not clear to me. I thought you were going to get clarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The answer by the General is that all those things that are mentioned there are things that are ordered by the Chief of the General Staff. Further down, he then says: "Because these are the elements that constitute preparations for combat. When it comes to the use of the force for which it was prepared, it doesn't have the right because this is within the exclusive purview of the supreme commander." Now, he has said, amongst others, combat can be ordered by the Chief of the Staff. Now he is saying combat can be ordered by the supreme commander only. Because all the other things are in preparation for combat. So I -- so I'm not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, there has been a misunderstanding due to interpretation. Can you provide an additional explanation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, since the Chief of the General Staff was tasked -- or, rather, responsible for the preparation of the forces of Yugoslavia, for its use in the course of those preparations, when it come to the contents of the preparations, this means training, education, the verification of combat readiness, the verification of mobilisation readiness, and other such activities. However, this excludes the engagement in war in -- or in combat. Such a war use could be ordered only by the President of the Republic. Let me provide an additional clarification. The Chief of the General Staff brought the forces up to the level or standard for use. The act of use, however, is something that is within the purview of the President of the Republic, and the President of the Republic had the exclusive right to issue an order for engagement. I don't know if I made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to Article 6 immediately and things will become even clearer. Can you please analyse the first two articles -- first two paragraphs of Article 6. Paragraph (1) and paragraph (2).

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Article 6 elaborates what I've already stated, and that is that the Chief of General Staff, in keeping with his authorities in the discharge of his duties, shall carry out his duties by issuing rules, orders, commands, instructions, and other documents. When it comes to the commanding officers of units and institutions of the General Staff and lower ranking officers, commanders of the forces corps, divisions and brigades, shall command their units in accordance with the law and the command documents issued by their superior officers. And for the Chief of General Staff, the superior officer is the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me just make a correction in the transcript. I can see that you were reading --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There's no reference to General Staff in paragraph 2 only units and institutions. The command of units and institutions.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you asked me to comment upon the article, not to read it, and I respected quite consistently what you asked me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. And when it comes to the General Staff, who is its commander?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The commander of the General Staff is the President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council, in accordance with the constitution, the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia, the Law on the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the military doctrine of the Army of Yugoslavia, would you say that the Law on the Army or any other regulation provides for the term "daily operative command"?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Our military [indiscernible] does not recognise in its work the term "operative daily command." We have command at strategic, operative, and tactical levels. As for the so-called daily operative command, in our vocabulary, that would be the method of work of the Chief of General Staff or unit commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And let me try and conclude. General Perisic, as the Chief of General Staff, was he authorised to command and use the units of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could he transfer any of the duties that he himself did not have onto somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me be very precise, because of the English interpretation. My question, on page 16, line 3, I'll repeat the question. I know that this is a problem for the interpreters, all the terms, and I will try and be very precise but I repeat my question for the clarity of understanding. General Perisic, as the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, was he authorised to order the use of the units of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The legislator was clear when he said, in the law, the commander of the Army of Yugoslavia was the President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will no longer need this document at the moment, but I believe that we will be able to come back to it and illustrate. I will now move on to the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and its structure and authorities, but I would like to do it by showing the witness a number of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is that answer, at line 17, an answer to your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who was the supreme commander, not everything may have been recorded in the transcript. The supreme commander of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The legislator didn't explicitly stipulate in any provision of the constitution or the law that it is the -- or, rather, who is the supreme commander. But it says that the President of the Republic, in accordance with the decisions taken by the Supreme Defence Council, commands the army, and since there is no part of the chain of command above him, it follows clearly that the one at the top is the supreme commander. That's how we interpreted it in 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm finding it difficult to follow this. I am -- I asked you if ... at page 16, line 17 -- or let me go to line 14. You asked: "General Perisic, as the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, was he authorised to order the use of the units of the Army of Yugoslavia?" The answer is: "The legislator was clear when he said, in law, commander in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Council" -- I don't know what --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I see that this is wrong. It's wrong in English. Let me try to be as precise as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will have to return to the question, General. I'll try to phrase it as simply as possible and I expect your answer to be such. My question was: Did General Perisic, as Chief of Staff of the VJ, have the authority to order the use of the units of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Not under the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who has the legal power to order the use of units?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The legislator vested the exclusive -- that exclusive right in the President of the Republic in his capacity of president of the Supreme Defence Council. That is his inalienable right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that in keeping with the principle of the unity of command that we mentioned with regard to Article 3?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the very thing. It may seem confusing that now the Supreme Defence Council comes into play as a collective organ, but, on the other hand, only one person is the commander. The Supreme Defence Council, as a collective organ, takes decisions jointly through discussion, and in keeping with the decision taking -- taken, and respecting the principle of unity of command, which says that only one person can be in command, that person is the President of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it clear now, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I just wanted that question to be answered, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will now move on to another topic, and that is the functioning of the General Staff of the VJ. My first question to you, General is: How were the structure and the purview of the General Staff of the armed forces of the Army of Yugoslavia regulated?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The structure and purview of the organisational bodies of the General Staff of the VJ was laid out by the Chief of General Staff, by his order about the tasks of the organisational units of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see pages 1 and 2 of document -- of 65 ter document 01114D. Your Honours, while we're waiting for the document, let me say that this is a rather lengthy document of some 30-odd pages. I didn't wish to tender the entire document initially, but now I understand that it is very important also with regard to the witnesses to come yet. And we don't have a complete English translation at the time being, but it will be completed soon. What we will deal with now is a part which has been assigned another 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now take look at the screen. I see that the pages don't match. And the page that we have in B/C/S, is this the order about the purview that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, the first page. But if you allow me, Mr. Lukic, let me ask to you move this closer to me, because I cannot get up all the time to read from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I prepared hard copies for you of all documents except for that one that we discussed earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Except, Mr. Lukic, that what we see on B/C/S side of the screen looks like the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And on the English side, we don't see the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that. I also wanted to see the cover page of the English version. I would like to see document 65 ter D00376D, both the B/C/S and English versions, which is what the witness has in front of him, only under a different number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What -- if you're now calling for --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I give up the previously called document for the time being. I apologise to everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... not going to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not yet. Page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, what we can see now --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but could we go back to the previous page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see on the screen the order on the purview of organisational units of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. Isn't that so? And who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: It was signed by the Chief of Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, Colonel General Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we -- it says below that this order shall take effect on the day it is issued. Or, rather: "On the day of this order taking effect, the rule book, et cetera, shall cease to be in force." When was this order issued?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: It was issued on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreters would like the date to be repeated, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the date.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The order was registered in the log-book of the 3rd Administration of the sector for replenishment, mobilisation and systemic affairs on 25th of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And where is that date on this document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you see now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. After the scrolling.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now move to page 2, general provisions. Can you say a few general comments about this document and then we will analyse it. What is this thing we're discussing?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Based on his legal authorities, the Chief of General Staff issued an order, by which he lays out in detail the rights, duties, and authority of the leading persons in the General Staff and the -- their organisational units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first chapter, general provisions, contains Article 2 and this is basically the -- a -- a copy of the legal provision that we saw in the law, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please comment Article 5 of the general provisions. To who does this article refer and what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Article 5 literally reads: "Command, in terms of this order, represents the function of integrated control of subordinate commands, units and institutions." That means that the Chief of General Staff can command his subordinates, give them duties and tasks, request reports and information about the carrying out of the duties assigned to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And we will see later for each section who has command authority over who; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please comment on Article 6.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Article 6 of the general provisions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the general provisions.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Article 6 of the general provisions reads: "Organisational units may not transfer affairs from their competence to VJ commands, units and institutions, unless authorised to do so." If you -- if the Chamber will allow me, I am going to clarify. Any obligation of mine that stems from this order cannot be transferred or delegated by me to anybody else. That is the untransferable right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The following chapter reads: The competences of the officers of organisational units of the General Staff of the VJ. Several positions or functions are mentioned here. Why isn't the Chief of Staff one of these? Instead it starts with the Deputy Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: This order is issued by the Chief of General Staff, and whatever he orders refers to his subordinates but not to himself. His duties are defined by a higher-ranking legal act.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. We will return to this document. But to facilitate the understanding of the remainder of the document, I would like to us take a look at some schematics. I believe that will be easier. What types of organisational units are there in the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The General Staff of the VJ, organisationally and in establishment terms, is structured on -- based on sections and administrations. So it has sections, departments, and other units. So you have -- when you asked me about my duties in the General Staff, I started with that of administrative officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will later tender this document, but I would like to see now 65 ter document 00804.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At what stage do you plan to tender this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A bit later today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked for a Defence document, a Defence document, 65 ter 0804D. To avoid any confusion, we marked all of our documents, all of our 65 ter documents with a D at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While this is being done, did the General Staff, in the organisational terms, undergo changes in the structure from the moment the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was created and its army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. From 1992, when the ministry was separated from the General Staff, in the course of the next several years, there was an ongoing process to build up the organisation and establishment structure. In the process of separation, many things in the system of command and control of the organisation were seen as being controversial. So gradually, as the situation allowed, we improved and built up on the organisation. That's why you will come across a lot of schematics starting with the sector --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that, but let's look at the illustration first. You have a Serbian version in front of you. This is a schematic dated 15 June 1993. Do you have that in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: And could this please be --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Hold on just for a moment. We'll give you a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have four schematics for the witness, and we would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to follow on the screen. Could you please put the English version on the screen for the Trial Chamber and everybody else in the courtroom, and the witness will be provided with hard copies in B/C/S. Let's just wait a moment for the English version to be brought back onto the screen for everybody in the courtroom. I believe that this version is too small for the Trial Chamber to be able to follow. You have to blow it up a little. Although General Perisic does not have the schematic in front of him, I'm sure he know what is we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, this schematic dates back from -- back to June 1993. Could you please tell us in a few words, in general terms, what the composition of the General Staff was. You don't have to describe everything in detail. Just describe the structure.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The Chief of General Staff, at that time, was linked to the sector for operations and staff; sector for organisation, recruitment and information; the logistics sector; personnel administration; information and moral guidance department; security administration; intelligence administration; and VJ inspection. All these were directly linked to him, as well as the department for liaising with international military representatives and his own office. So this is the most immediate link in the chain of command for the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And for the Trial Chamber to be able to follow the first next major change that happened, what was the problem within the schematic and what was changed subsequently? What elements or -- maybe I should put on the screen the next schematic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I have them in hard copy. With the permission of the Trial Chamber, I would say that here you can see that in the sector for operations and staff affairs there are branch administrations which are responsible for branches in depth. For example, the administration for land army accounts for 80 per cent of the Army of Yugoslavia; the air force administration accounts for 15 per cent; and navy accounts for 8 per cent. And thus the leading personnel --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness is now dealing with the first column on the left-hand side. In the sector for operations, reference is made to land forces administration, air force administration, and navy operation -- administrations. [In English] In that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you're talking about the different branches or services, you mean three services in the military, or different branches?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I am referring to them, meaning that the Army of Yugoslavia was composed three different branches: Land forces, air force, and navy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And at that time --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: And now -- and when we took over the organisation, which meant that we were separated from the General Staff, such administrations which were actually sectors in the ministry, we transformed them into administrations which aggravated --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you in order to avoid confusion and also we have the interpretation. You mean in the period when there was the Secretariat for National Defence, those were sectors within the National Secretariat, and then in this schematic you transformed them into administrations within the framework of the first sector? Just for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, bearing in mind the aggravating circumstance you will see in the following schematic that, from the sector for operations and staff affairs, we brought those administrations up to a higher level and linked them up directly to the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Could we please --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would firstly like to tender this document into evidence before I do anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to the admission of this document at this time. We know nothing about the source of this document. We know nothing about who made it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe the witness can help us and tell us whether he knows who drafted the schematics that we are currently discussing?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: These schematics were prepared by the General Staff within the framework of the project to transform the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, and they were drafted by the entire General Staff under the leadership of the chief of the sector for operations and staff affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And let me add to that, Your Honours, in the document of the order, there is a schematic that accompanies the 1994 order. I intentionally provided a bigger expert [as interpreted] for us to peruse but let me repeat that one part of the entire order is also the schematic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm not sure which document Mr. Lukic is referring to now. We're dealing with 803D; isn't that correct? Or 804?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 804D [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. In any event, I believe that the witness corroborated the authenticity of the document and that the document can therefore be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The only problem is the witness says it was drawn by the General Staff. You know, he doesn't tell us who in the Staff drew this document. He says -- you know, if you read at page 27, line 10: "The schematics were prepared by the General Staff within the framework of the project to transform the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, and they were drafted by the entire General Staff under the leadership of the chief of the sector for operations and staff affairs." I'm not quite sure whether he tells us who drafted this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume, Your Honours, that we should not maintain the standard of knowing exactly who the author of each and every document is. As for the authenticity of this document, we have a competent witness who confirms that this was drafted by a whole body, and I believe that when it comes to the authenticity that this is relevant and enough for a document to be admitted. We have had a lot of Prosecution documents admitted without any of the witnesses being able to ascertain which person exactly drafted the document but were able to confirm its authenticity. You are here to be the judge of the witness's capability to confirm the authenticity of the document. He told us that the document was drafted by the entire General Staff. Maybe Mr. Simic has something to add.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The way it was translated to me was that the entire General Staff became the sector for operations and staff affairs. I didn't say that. I state at this point that within the process of transformation, the coordinating role, the main role was assumed by the sector for operations and staff affairs. However, that sector was not omnipotent. In coordination with other sectors it came by and arrived at optimum solutions for particular schematics that we see here at the moment in front of us. And these schematics were subsequently changed and they assumed their final shape in the year 1994, pursuant to an order of the Chief of the General Staff about the authorities and competencies of the organisational units of the General Staff. The schematics show a certain evolution in the organisational buildup and improvement of the General Staff structure. I don't know whether I have managed to make myself clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any comments from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, are you able to tell us, in brief, what the witness was saying here? I'm not quite sure I understand. We're dealing here with --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I believe that the witness has tried to explain a factual position and he has tried to explain why the structure of the General Staff had to be changed. But I adhere to my original comment. The witness said that the schematic was drafted by the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia which confirms the authenticity of the document. We can't go on and try to ascertain who the individual author of each and every document is. I believe that the authenticity of the document has been corroborated sufficiently for the document to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The document shall be assigned Exhibit D195. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the break, I would like to go over the second schematic, just briefly, to maintain the line of questioning. Or maybe -- or perhaps we should have the break first, Your Honours, and then come back to the second schematic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to come back to this one, because I don't know what it is telling me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you wanted to clarify something about the schematic additionally, or maybe I can pass on to the next one and then I believe what the witness said will become fully clear, because the witness was already explaining things that can be found in the following schematic, so either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, we were looking at the schematic from June 1993, and you said that the branches of the military were -- were in the first sector. Now, let's, please, see the 65 ter Defence document, 00805D. And please comment briefly on the changes as compared to the previous state which -- which refers to June 1993. Let me just check whether we have the English version of the document for the Trial Chamber to be able to follow. You have in front of you this document from December 1993. And what kind of changes were made to the organisational structure of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: In the improvement of the organisational structure, which we call transformation, the greatest change occurred in the sector for operational and staff affairs. Earlier, this sector contained the land forces administration. But now, as we can see from the schematic, this -- this is an sector for the land forces, which has its service administrations. Likewise, in the earlier schematic, we had the air force and anti-aircraft defence administration within this sector, but now, after the changes, we can see there is a sector for the air force and anti-aircraft defence, which sector has its administrations -- administrations. Furthermore, we can observe the same in the navy administration. In the more recent version, it has grown into a sector for the navy. These are the most significant changes that affected the organisation of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something that matters to me for the Defence. We don't need to call up the previous schematic but we can see the intelligence administration as an independent administration directly subordinate to the chief. What happened to the intelligence administration in this transformation as we see in this schematic from December 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The intelligence administration, in the previous schematic, which reported to the Federal Secretariat of People's Defence, was autonomous or independent. We saw that the intelligence administration must be integrated with the operations officer, and it became -- it has become part of the sector for operational and staff affairs. It become an organisational unit of that sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How -- what is it called here in this schematic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: It's called the 2nd Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The intelligence administration was also called -- often called the 2nd Administration, right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We also see here some slight changes. Among others, we can see the position of Deputy Chief of General Staff. How come?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Due to the complexity of affairs and due to the large workload on the General Staff at the time, the solution was introduced to establish the position of Deputy Chief of General Staff as a person to coordinate some organisational units and, thus, he will be able to present to the Chief of General Staff semi-finalised products, to call them that, without -- so that the Chief of General Staff doesn't have to deal with everything from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There's another organisational unit important to us here. The previous department for liaison with international military representatives here becomes the administration for liaison with international military representatives. I apologise for putting leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, can you see that clearly from the schematic. I didn't consider it necessary to mention it. This department became an administration because the Chief of General Staff assigned more a complex task to that organisational unit. Otherwise, the tasks remained the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I will ask you something that I didn't ask you in the proofing, so if you don't remember, don't reply. Do you know who headed the individual sectors or administration in 1993 and the two years to follow? Do you remember who was the head of this administration for liaison with international military representatives?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I believe it was Colonel Dragan Vuksic, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I think too. Who was the head of the your sector for operational staff affairs?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: If you're asking me only about the period when General Perisic was there, there were General Polic, General Blagoje Kovacevic, General Martinovic, and I subsequently left the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who was the head of the security administration?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Throughout that period, Colonel Aleksandar Dimitrijevic was the head of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who you happen to know who the head of the logistics sector was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: It was General Djukic in the earliest period. After Djukic there was Milovanovic, then Sljivic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But Djukic was before the transformation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the earliest period. That's why I called it that. Before the transformation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know who was the head of the office of the Chief of General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The office of the Chief of General Staff was headed by several persons in sequence. There were Colonel Bojovic, Colonel Zivanovic, who later became General. And there was another, but I can't remember his name now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sinisa --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: For a while, General Milovanovic and Sinisa Borovic for the most time and there was one more, but I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this schematic into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will simply make the same objection that I made to the last document, as we have no evidence as to who actually produced this. Just for the record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only repeat my previous reply. The witness knows that this document originates from the General Staff and I believe that sufficiently establishes the authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't testify, Mr. Lukic. You haven't asked that question to this witness [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I didn't ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... you can't just say I will repeat what I said earlier. You have got to get this witness to authenticate this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know the origin of the schematic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I feel the need to additionally clarify the methodology of the production of this document, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It cannot be said that the -- one person is the author of the entire document. Based on the order issued by the 1st Administration of the sector for operational staff affairs to make a new organisational structure of the General Staff, all organisational units submit their respective proposals to the sector for organisation, manning, and ... and mobilisation systemic issues. Then what ensued is a discussion at the level of organisational units and the amended proposals are submitted to the Chief of General Staff, to who they were presented. What was -- he is informed of what was harmonised and what was not, and then it is up to him to decide. Based on that decision, the administration for organisation and manning produces the document in accordance with the order of the Chief of General Staff. I hope that I was being clear enough now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, what the witness has just explained then really raises some additional issues. How do we know then that what we're seeing here, what is being offered by the Defence was the final version that was approved by the Chief of the General Staff? We've heard no evidence of that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I merely asked the witness whether this document was produced in the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, then the issue, Your Honour, goes to probative value. If we don't know whether this was the final version that was approved by the Chief of the General Staff, then what probative value would this document have in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if the Prosecution challenges the authenticity, that is one thing. The witness explained the structure, and that it was in full correspondence, it fully matched the schematic, and that this schematic was made by the General Staff. The witness stated that this is a reflection of the organisational structure of the General Staff at the time. And this schematic was produced in the General Staff, and I believe that it is admissible as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, this may very well be one of the proposals that the witness described a few moments ago. We don't know whether this version was accepted as the proper version by the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can't you solve that but just asking the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I needn't say at all that this is the version as signed by the Chief of General Staff. This witness was saying that this version, this document, was made in the General Staff as the document that reflected the functioning of the General Staff at that time. If I had a document signed by the Chief of General Staff, that would be one thing. But this is a schematic which shows that this document was produced in the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question is not whether it was signed by the General Staff [sic]. It is whether he approved it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, do you know whether General Perisic approved such a schematic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. This schematic is one of the appendices that we used at the time while we were working on these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if this document -- if this schematic was used as an appendix while documents were being worked on, that does not necessarily indicate that this is a final version that was approved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute, wait a minute. Mr. -- Mr. Simic, did you indicate at the beginning, when you started with these schematics, were they attached to an order by the Chief of General Staff or are they just separate documents? They're not attached to anything. Because I thought, when you started, there was an order, and then there was the schematics which were attachments. Can you just correct me there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said both. The methodology of work was such that the operations administration issues a systemic order as to what must be done by organisational units. It is clear it is defined that each has to submit a proposal on behalf of its organisational unit as to the structure of the future General Staff. Based on that order of the Chief of General Staff, the organisational units submit their own proposals to the sector for organisation and manning, and based on all these proposals, a discussion takes place about what is good, what isn't, what should be changed, et cetera, and we come up with a single position. Based on that, the organisational sector takes a decision which will be signed by the Chief of General Staff with these appendices but not all of them, because it didn't all happen at the same moment. It -- it went on over a period of time. So one schematic applies to one period, another to another period, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please listen to my question and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I maybe be able to help before you ask your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I asked a question and I'd like it to be answered. Listen to my question very carefully. My question to you is: As you started testifying about the schematics, I got the impression that these schematics are attachments to the order issued by the General -- the Chief of the General Staff. Am I right in saying so, or am I wrong? Are they part of a document that forms the order that was issued by the Chief of the General Staff? Your answer is going to be yes, or no, or I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to put another question before your final decision about the authenticity of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the B/C/S version of this document on the screen, please. Could the stamp please be blown up? It's in the right-hand side corner. This is for the witness to read and tell us whose stamp this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you possibly read --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The Republic of Serbia, Ministry of Defence, Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where would a document of this kind and with this stamp originate from?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because it is the successor of --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is the successor of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you say it originates from the minister of defence? It doesn't originate from the office of the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The office of the Chief of General Staff is a miniature unit in the organisation and it could not be responsible for such a complex task. There are tactical subjects responsible for that. It originates from the minister of defence because at that time we inherited that from the minister of defence, General Zivota Panic was still the Chief of General Staff and the other Panic was minister of defence. The two had not been separated at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to clarify and answer your question, but I -- for that, I would need to send the witness out of the courtroom. I would like to avoid any further confusion but I don't want the discussion to take place in front of the witness. So can the witness please be removed for a couple of minutes, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It will not be necessary. The document is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wish -- I would like to clarify one more thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... trouble is, are you going to take the witness-stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. There's no need for the witness to leave, I agree. But I would like to clarify that all documents that bear this stamp, and the Prosecutor knows it, originate from the archives of the Ministry of Serbia. That's where the archives are housed. All the documents that the OTP received from the National Council for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal originate from the archives of the Ministry of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have already given a ruling. Thanks for the explanation. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit D196.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, let's look at another table very briefly. It's 65 ter, for the next sequence of transformations, 65 ter 00803D. 12 May 1994 is the date that this table bears. And -- just briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And can we -- we do see the B/C/S [Overlapping speakers] ... it has a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation][Overlapping speakers] ... yes, of course. Yes, of course. Of course, can we have the English, please, yes. Could we have the English version on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a few words with regard to the changes on the previous structure of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Which schematic do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't have that schematic, as far as I can tell. The month of May. I have the month of June 1993; December 1993; 12 May 1994. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where is that date on this English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could move to the right? Could you move the document to the right? No, sorry, to the left, in order to display the date in the right upper corner. Now I've just been told that there's no date, although in the B/C/S there is a date, Your Honours. Maybe we can display the official translation -- or, rather, the B/C/S original. Can you see the date in the upper right-hand side corner?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, I can see. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I can assist, on the bottom of page 3 of my English translation, there is an date, or at least there seems to be a footer, which describes the document and gives the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. We don't see that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please -- all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Witness, where do you see a difference, if you do?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Can you -- can I have it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The English version only a few sentences.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: In this schematic, in our further work, a need arose for the organisational unit to be called by its proper name. For example, sector for operations and staff affairs. And the chief who covered that establishment post was then called the assistant Chief of General Staff for operations and staff affairs. Accordingly, a need also arose for a chief himself, because of the technical requirements he had, and the coordination with his subordinates, to exist a miniature organ that we called a sector for operations and staff affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is not of a -- any consequence for our case -- for our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Even though it is of no consequence to your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, what the witness has just told us is enough. I don't want to pursue the matter any further. He told us that there were changes indeed within the sector, within the framework of the sector, and that suffices. I don't want to pursue the matter any further. I would like to speed things along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D197. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the last schematic, could we have it on the screen? 65 ter 00806D, dated 29 December 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have a hard copy, General, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will have just one question with regard this schematic, something that I want to hear from you. We saw that, during the previous period, the intelligence administration, that you also called the 2nd Administration, was part of the sector for operations and staff affairs. Could you tell us what happened to it as a result of this transformation that took place in December 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The intelligence administration or the 2nd Administration for intelligence, or just the 2nd Administration as it was referred to in the previous schematic, a need arose for the Chief of General Staff to have that administration directly linked to him so as to be able to communicate with it without any mediators and to receive information first-hand. And that's why this was removed from the sector for operations and staff affairs, and became directly attached to the Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It became an independent administration?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. It became an independent administration within the General Staff, which means that one step was skipped within the chain of command and the Chief of General Staff received direct information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was the head of the intelligence administration during that period of time that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down, slow down. [Microphone not activated]. You may answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You may answer.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: Branko Krga, General Branko Krga. And later on, he became the Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please tender this document into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D198. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now we shall go back to the order on the authorities of organisational units but we will be dealing exclusively with your sector and your administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before that, Your Honours, I would like to refer to the document that we looked at as a general introduction. The number is D176D [as interpreted] to be tendered into evidence, that was the first part of that order, and now we will be dealing with the second part of that order and we will call it up on the screen. I would like that tender 00376D into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 00376D, the document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D199. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, let's talk about the sector where you spent most of your career in the General Staff, and especially about its 1st Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce 65 ter 0114D. B/C/S page 7; English page 1. Let me repeat, 1114.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How many 1s?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] 1114D. [Interpretation] Page 7 in B/C/S, please; page 1 in English, please. Could you please move the B/C/S version to the left? I am interested in bullet point 16. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's analyse the sector for operations and staff affairs. General, you can see here what the basic functions of the sector are. Could you please explain in your own words what the significance of the sector was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
utterances.text: The sector for operations and staff affairs unified and coordinated the activities of its organisational units when it came to the performance and discharge of tasks and duties. Actually, it was a staff organ of the General Staff. And in this particular schematic, you can see that it was dealing with the tasks pertaining to planning, the engagement and combat readiness, planning the development of the VJ, combat training and education, as well as intelligence support to the VJ. This is -- this is where a different administration was -- or, rather, the 2nd Administration was still part of that sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. What was the place of the 1st Administration within the framework of this sector?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG SIMIC
